parole.significato: Synonym of common broom (“Cytisus scoparius”).
parole.testo: From Cornish banadhel (“broom”).

parole.significato: A shed for cattle or sheep.
parole.testo: From Cornish bowji (“cowshed”).

parole.significato: To dunk or immerse (into water, for remedial purposes).
parole.testo: Ultimately borrowed from Cornish beudhi or Breton beuziñ (“to drown”).

parole.significato: A type of flatfish, Scophthalmus rhombus.
parole.testo: Possibly from Cornish brilli (“mackerel”), from brithelli, plural of brithel (“mackerel”), from brith (“spotted”), from Proto-Brythonic *briθ.

parole.significato: A storm spirit in Cornish folklore, traditionally believed to inhabit mines and coastal communities.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Cornish bocka. Doublet of pooka and puck.

parole.significato: A person who eats or drinks a substantial amount.
parole.testo: From Cornish boos (“food, meal, fare”) + gut.

parole.significato: An exploratory trench used when first digging a mine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Cornish koghyn (“exploratory trench”), with spelling likely influenced by etymology 1.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Cornwall, a county of southwest England.
parole.testo: From Corn(wall) + -ish, from Cornish Kernewek, Kernowek.

parole.significato: A trench in solid rock intersected by pits which reveals mineral veins.
parole.testo: Presumably from Cornish kodha (“to fall, happen”) + sten (“tin”).

parole.significato: To complain; to whine; to moan.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Cornish krena (“to tremble”).

parole.significato: An ailing or sickly person.
parole.testo: From creen (“to complain”) + -er, from Cornish krena (“to tremble”).

parole.significato: Sift with a sieve.
parole.testo: From Cornish dyllo (“sift with a sieve”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to certain veins of feldspathic or porphyritic rock crossing metalliferous veins in the mining districts…
parole.testo: From a Cornish word, perhaps Cornish elven, elvan (“spark”) because the hard rock could be struck to spark fire.

parole.significato: A Cornish souterrain, an underground, dry-stone-walled chamber open on two ends.
parole.testo: From Cornish fogo (“cave”); compare vug.

parole.significato: A traditional dance held on Flora Day in Helston, Cornwall.
parole.testo: Probably from Cornish fer.

parole.significato: Rust-coloured (weatherized and oxidized) rock or mineral deposits, forming the upper part or outcrop of a metallic vein.
parole.testo: Borrowed in the 1770s from Cornish gossen, from gōs (“blood”), from Old Cornish guit (compare Proto-Celtic *wolis).

parole.significato: A decomposed granite, forming a mass of sandy gravel, found in tin lodes in Cornwall.
parole.testo: From Cornish growan (“gravel”). Compare Armorican grouan (“gravel”), Cornish grow (“gravel, sand”).

parole.significato: A vacant space left in the ground after a lode has been mined.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Cornish gonis (“gunnies”).

parole.significato: A cake of Cornish origin, made with flour, lard, butter, milk, sugar, and raisins.
parole.testo: Folk-etymological alteration of hevva cake; ultimately from Cornish hedva (“swarm, shoal”).

parole.significato: A pile of rocks.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Cornish karn. Doublet of cairn.

parole.significato: To sift using a sieve, particularly in mining tin or silver.
parole.testo: Clipping of dillue (“sift with a sieve”), from Cornish dyllo (“sift with a sieve”).

parole.significato: An ant.
parole.testo: From Cornish moryon. Cognate with Breton merien and Welsh myrion.

parole.significato: A large pelagic predatory shark, Lamna nasus, of the Atlantic.
parole.testo: Unclear, but likely from Cornish porth (“harbor”) + bugel (“shepherd”), with the latter element either influenced by English beagle or in fact formed from it, with only the first element truly being from Cornish.

parole.significato: A soft, white clay.
parole.testo: From Cornish pri (“clay”), possibly + -an (adjective-forming suffix) with later nominalization. Not, however, derived from Cornish prien (“clay ground”), which is itself a borrowing of pryan from English.

parole.significato: A frog or toad.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Cornish kwilkyn (“frog”).

parole.significato: A hare.
parole.testo: From Cornish skovarnek.

parole.significato: A vein of tin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Cornish scoren.

parole.significato: In Cornish folklore, a malicious spirit in the form of a wizened old man.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Cornish spyrysyon (“spirits; fairies”).

parole.significato: Irritable or angry.
parole.testo: From Cornish tesek (“irritable, hot”).

parole.significato: A sand dune.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Cornish tewyn.

parole.significato: A shovel used in cleansing ore.
parole.testo: From Cornish.

parole.significato: A small to medium-sized cavity inside rock that may be formed through a variety of processes.
parole.testo: From Cornish vooga (“cave”); compare fogou.

parole.significato: A mine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Cornish hwel.

parole.significato: Any one of numerous edible, marine, spiny-finned fishes of the family Labridae, of which several species are found in t…
parole.testo: Plural of dialectal (Cornwall) wrah, wraugh, wrath, from Cornish wragh (“old woman, hag; wrasse”), lenited form of gwragh.

parole.significato: A deep and narrow sea-inlet in the British Isles, especially Cornwall and the south-west, cut by erosion into sea-cliff…
parole.testo: From Cornish sâwn, sawan (“chasm”). Cognate with Welsh safn (“mouth”), Breton staoñ (“palate”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; perhaps; or from; modificatore <unc> nel legame
parole.significato: A short, heavy club, often of wood, which is thicker or loaded at one end.
parole.testo: First attested in 1730. Origin uncertain, perhaps of Cornish origin (recorded as blogon c. 1450) or from Middle French bougeon, a diminutive of bouge (“club, stick”).
